transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, thanks for seeing me. I suppose what brought me in is... I find myself checking the same boxes, lists, and drawers around the condo over and over before I can move on to whatever I'm doing. 

I know perfectly well I already looked. But I just keep doing it, even when my wife is waiting for me to just leave it be. It's getting to be a bit tiresome, so I figured I should come talk to someone about it.
When you feel the urge to check again, is it mainly because you're anxious something bad might happen if you don't, or because you don't trust that you did it correctly the first time?

Well, I suppose it's more about these nagging thoughts I keep getting. I'll just be going about my day, and suddenly I worry that I might have accidentally thrown away something important from my old teaching files, or maybe I put a needed tool in the wrong box. 

I tell myself it's highly unlikely I did that, but... the thought just comes back anyway. It makes it very hard to just settle down until I go look. So I guess it's less about some terrible disaster happening, and more that I just don't trust I didn't make a mistake the first time around.

Would you say this need to double-check things feels like an unwanted urge that bothers you, or does it feel more like part of your general personality—like you've always needed things to be done in a very precise, orderly way across many parts of your life?

I wouldn't say it's part of my personality, no. I've never been someone who needed everything lined up perfectly or... or organized in a strict way. I mean, I like things tidy enough, but this checking thing... it feels different. It's definitely unwanted. It just bothers me that I can't shake the thought without going back to look, even though I know I don't really need to. It's more of a nuisance that gets in the way, not just how I prefer to do things.

latest_inference.note: Patient explicitly denies lifelong perfectionism or rigid orderliness, describing the checking as an unwanted, intrusive, ego-dystonic urge rather than a personality trait—ruling out F60.5 (OCPD) and supporting F42 (OCD).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports recurrent, unwanted intrusive thoughts (fear of having made a mistake, e.g., discarding something important) that are recognized as excessive and irrational, coupled with repetitive checking behaviors performed to reduce the distress caused by these thoughts. The patient explicitly denies that this pattern reflects a longstanding personality trait of orderliness or perfectionism, distinguishing it from Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (F60.5). The behaviors are ego-dystonic, time-consuming, and cause functional friction (e.g., delaying activities, frustrating his wife), consistent with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42) rather than a generalized anxiety pattern (F41.1), which would not typically involve specific ritualistic compulsions tied to discrete obsessions.

Thoughts experienced as unwanted and intrusive
Repeated checking of boxes, lists, and drawers
Checking behavior performed despite knowing it's unnecessary
Behavior performed to neutralize obsessive doubt rather than for gratification
Patient recognizes the checking as excessive and unreasonable
Patient explicitly states this is not a personality trait or preference for order
Behavior described as a 'nuisance' rather than an identity-consistent trait

additional_requirements: Behavior distinguished from Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder by patient's denial of general need for order/control across life domains
Compulsions are directly linked to specific obsessive doubts rather than generalized anxiety
